Fast-Forwarding Your Life - The Harm of Social Media

What we lose at the expense of a product that makes us mistake convenience for connection

The mental cloud we maintain just for a slice of 'conneciton'

The Fast-Forward Button

Before I go into anything, I want you to imagine something for me: a teenager who, at the young age of about 12 to 13, is given an all powerful remote which allows them to fast-forward through the boring and mundane parts of life. 

  For this person - the user of the remote - they cannot pause or rewind time. Fast forwarding is the only use case, and it presents the users eyes with a sort of ‘fast-forward screen’ which is filled with random clippings and images just like fast-forwarding a movie or show in Netflix. Too many images for the remote-user to remember for the most part.   

Now, our dear User has those ‘boring’ moments of life that we all do, like waiting for the toast to pop out of the toaster, the kettle to boil, traffic in front of the bus to move, or just siting in the waiting room at the doctors. Naturally, the User figures the remote would be useful for skipping ahead of these times. This skipping continues on whenever the User feels, and with this we start to see their perception of ‘what a boring moment is’ begin to change into a moment that should just be skipped. They are now fast-forwarding progressively more often. It’s not until the User hits 40 or 50 that they begin looking back on their life and come to the stark realization that they can’t recall too much of it, only the common fast-forward screens that were used to speed up moments.. It has now dawned on the user just how much time has been perceptually lost. 

The 2006 Adam Sandler film ‘Click’ is not what I am drawing similarities to, but rather that little brick you often have in your pocket, with certain apps being the fast-forward button on your very own remote.  

The Benefits of Boredom

Collectively, we reach for social media to satisfy ourself in the quiet and uninteresting moments of our life. The issue is that, other than obvious effects of social media like a reduced attention span, emotional hijacking, algorithmic manipulation, and more - when we skip the quiet and potentially boring parts of life we are skipping life itself.  Before our boredom could be turned off like a light switch, it would force us to have spontaneous thoughts, in which would allow us better time to observe and interpret the world and also ourselves as individuals. We are our thoughts and without them we are simply flesh just moving on by without care or our own true fulfillment. According to studies done by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), CNN, Science Direct, etc, the average age now for social media sign-ups is roughly 12-13 years old.  Society is being bred to believe that this is normal when it is not.

I think it’s worth noting that a lot of parents prevent or discourage their kids from using social media for the fear of their kid seeing inappropriate things online, which I agree is a deterring factor though I just don’t think it’s worth overshadowing the psychological aspect of using social media and constantly consuming short form content, especially at a young age with a developing mind. I don’t know how this isn’t talked about enough, as it’s like handing your kid an endless supply of cigarettes and Playboy magazines and worrying simply over the content they’ll see rather then the addictions they may easily form and lose time to.

  There are too many people in my life of whom I could not imagine just sitting down on their couch and doing nothing but thinking and pondering - exploring their self identity. I know I often substitute these moments for social media myself, and as much as I’d like to say “I feel guilty but I’m aware of why this is wrong”, my guilt does not absolve me. If anything it just makes it worse, knowing the dangers or losing myself and still getting back on those apps.  

A Lack Of Connection

Now, a major factor keeping me to social media is that all my friends and family use it and it feels like such necessary form of connection to anyone. When I have tried to remove a lot of the people I used to know from social media, I was met with a fear of missing out which then lead to me feeling a lack of connection. The odd thing about this though was that this happened even with people I haven’t spoken to in ages, and that I know are different now than to who they were when we were closer.  I have had to come to terms with the realisation that your past self and your past connections shouldn’t be a defining factor in keeping your present and future self imprisoned to an app. 

There is also nothing wrong with getting the phone numbers of people you actually care about, and sending them a text every so often to check up on them. If they return the texts and are also the ones sending you the first text every now and then, I would say that is a clear indicator that they actually care. If they do not, and you often find yourself being the only one making any effort, then that should tell you what you probably already knew. Anyone can press a button to accept a follow request, but someone who cares will take the time to actually see how you are. 

Don’t mistake connection for convenience when it comes to social media.   

Addiction and Creation

Another major aspect against social media is that it truly is an addiction, all the way down to how our brain changes when using it and our behaviors surrounding it. I once heard someone say that if you took videos of everyone you saw scrolling social media in public, and then edited out the phones they were using, it would would look as though everyone is a drug addict just sitting there, staring at their hands while very still, for long periods on end. It does get to a certain point where you have to ask yourself: what’s really the difference in terms of time spent.  

Us humans are inherently creative creatures though it has become, once again, normalized to consume a far more outrageous amount of content than that of which we create. I like to write, I like to make pretty ammeter YouTube videos, I like to very, very amateurishly paint, but over all I like to create, and I found that the addictive aspect of social media just took so much time from me to do anything, let alone any time available for creation. Tying back to what I said before about our thoughts relating to our self identity, our creations are another major aspect of that too. Pieces that we have put out into the world in some way that wasn’t there before. In my own experience I have also seen so many people use social media without ever, and with no intent of ever, creating anything to post on it. Purely consuming. That scares me and it should scare you too.  

So What’s Next?  

The obvious answer, that I’m sure many people won’t like, is to get rid of this drug. Whether or not you intend on doing so is up to you, though I would recommend reading the following in the event that you might want to do so later on. It is so easy to delete your social media accounts as it only takes about a minute, but the hard part is changing your life to not revolve around the dopamine hits in those empty moments, because that is what is going to cause the most relapse. In my own experiences after deleting social media, I would get to a point where certain moments were too quiet and I would redownload the social media app I had just deleted. An important part of the journey of deleting your social media is working out what you’ll do next.  For some people, this may be a video game to ease them through the initial period right afterwards, and while I’m sure there are better things to do than gaming, I’m also certain that dopamine-wise it’ll be better than sitting on your phone, scrolling and consuming. For me, I find it best to spend more time writing, whether it is an informative piece or just a story that I come up with in my mind.   

One thing that I feel really is helping me to spend more time away from social media is this little blog website. The OnWiki. I have crafted my own little place on the internet where I can upload my pieces I write, will write, or wrote in the past and also a place to upload some photos. Surprisingly, one thing that I really find hard about trying to quit social media is that I just really want a public place to share some pictures I took, hence why I added the Collage button/page to this website. I have replaced my Instagram carousel posts and my digital sense of identity through liked videos with my very own Collage and my own opinions expressed through these posts, here on the Onwiki.   

My over arching point though is that for most people, you can’t expect to just jump head first - cold turkey -  into not using social media without having a clear reason for yourself and a way to replace the time spent on it. My hope is that this little opinion piece I have written will serve as the foundation of your reasoning, and that you’ll either take it into respect or do further research into it and eventually cut out those distracting and mind screwing aspects of your life. If you want your journey away from the tentacles of social media to be lasting and fruitful, having options for how to spend your time is essential. I can’t stress enough that these social media companies pay BILLIONS to have the best-of-the-best team of people from various fields around the world (including human psychology), all work to keep you on their app. 

By staying on social media, you are fighting a losing battle and that is truly what I have come to know and hope you will too, either now or in time.
